verses.note: God creates by speaking. The first thing Scripture shows about God's word is that it is effective: it does what it says. That conviction stands behind the prophets' "Thus says the LORD" and John's description of Christ as the Word.

The scene turns on the exact wording of God's word. Once the command is shrunk in generosity, sharpened in strictness, and softened in consequence, it is easier to set aside. Interpreters differ on whether ‘or touch it’ is a distortion or a well-meant fence around the command, but either way the conversation is now about a reshaped word.

God reveals his purpose to Noah before he acts. Amos 3:7 states the principle that the Lord does nothing without revealing his plan to his servants the prophets, and Peter calls Noah a preacher of righteousness (2 Peter 2:5).

The first time Scripture says the word of the LORD ‘came’ to someone, it comes to Abram in a vision. The prophetic word begins with the promise to Abraham, which is why later prophets keep returning to it.

God chooses to disclose his intentions to Abraham before acting. Amos 3:7 states the principle, and Jesus calls his disciples friends because he has made known to them what he heard from the Father (John 15:15). Abraham is called God's friend (2 Chronicles 20:7, Isaiah 41:8, James 2:23).
God speaks directly to a king outside the covenant family. Revelation in Genesis is not confined to the chosen line, even though its purpose here is to protect that line.

God speaks first and names himself before he asks anything. Jacob has done nothing to seek him, and the God who speaks identifies himself by his history with Jacob's family, so revelation comes as the continuation of promises already made.

God identifies himself by a place and an event, the pillar Jacob anointed and the vow he made there (28:18-22). The God who speaks now is the same God who spoke then, and he holds Jacob to what was said between them.
God gives what Jacob needs, a blessing and a name, but withholds what Jacob would control, his own name. Revelation in Scripture is always given at God's initiative and on his terms (Exodus 3:13-14).

Scripture holds together two truths: no one can see God's face and live (Exodus 33:20), and yet God does let himself be seen, in measure, by those he chooses. Jacob's amazement belongs with Gideon's and Manoah's (Judges 6:22-23, 13:22), and the New Testament says God is finally made known in the Son (John 1:18).

God is not named, but the paired dreams are the first hint in Joseph's story that God is speaking. Joseph later teaches Pharaoh that a doubled dream means the matter is fixed by God (41:32). Jacob's keeping of the word is the posture Luke describes in Mary, who "treasured up all these things" (Luke 2:19).

Joseph denies that dream interpretation is a human technique and says it belongs to God. Revelation in Scripture is God's gift, not the product of expertise, and Daniel will make the same claim before Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 2:27-28).
The narrator's confirmation follows the test later given for a true prophet: what he says comes to pass (Deuteronomy 18:22). Joseph's words prove to be God's.

Egypt's most learned men, with their manuals and training, cannot read a message God has sent. Scripture repeatedly sets divine revelation against the wisdom of the empires, as Isaiah mocks Pharaoh's senseless counselors (Isaiah 19:11) and Paul asks where the wise man of this age has gone (1 Corinthians 1:20).
Joseph insists that the power to interpret belongs to God alone and that God is willing to speak to a pagan king. Daniel will say nearly the same before Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 2:27-28, 2:30).

God reveals his purposes even to those outside his covenant people, and he does so for their good and the world's. The prophet Amos says the Lord does nothing without revealing his plan to his servants the prophets (Amos 3:7); here the servant is Joseph and the hearer is Pharaoh.
Repetition in revelation is a mark of confirmation, a principle that later appears in the law's requirement of two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15) and in Paul's use of it (2 Corinthians 13:1).

God's final recorded speech in Genesis comes to a man at the edge of the promised land, about to leave it. The next time God speaks in the biblical story, from the burning bush, he speaks to the people this family becomes, still in Egypt (Exodus 3:4-10).

Signs in Scripture do not replace the word; they confirm the messenger who brings it. The pattern continues in the New Testament, where God testifies to the message of salvation by signs and wonders (Hebrews 2:3-4).

The promise to teach Moses what to say is the pattern of prophecy: God's word placed in a human mouth. Jesus gives his disciples a similar promise when they must speak before rulers (Matthew 10:19-20).

The law begins as speech from God to a people who hear him. Israel's knowledge of God's will does not come from discovering the moral order by reflection but from being addressed, which is why Deuteronomy 4:12 stresses that they heard a voice and saw no form.
‘You have seen that I have spoken’ joins two senses: Israel experienced God's speech as an event it witnessed. Revelation here is both something heard and a public event in history.
The covenant is put in writing. God's words at Sinai are not left to memory but fixed on stone and scroll, the beginning of Scripture as a written witness that each generation could read.

God's word reaches the people through a man whose face shows where he has been. The radiance authenticates Moses' words as coming from God's presence, and the veil marks the difference between that presence and ordinary life in the camp.
Israel's knowledge of God's will does not come from technique but from God's own speech. The contrast is between reading signs and hearing a word.
Revelation through a human mediator is not a lesser form God settled for. He approves it as a mercy suited to people who cannot bear his unmediated presence.
The prophet's words are God's words given through a human mouth. This verse lies behind the church's conviction that Scripture is both a human and a divine word.
The prophet's task is to relay the whole word, including the parts that correct him. Nathan's obedience models the definition of a prophet in Deuteronomy 18:18.

The final state of the world is defined by knowledge of God filling everything. Habakkuk 2:14 repeats the line with ‘the knowledge of the glory of the LORD’. The Bible's hope is not only for peace but for God known everywhere, which is why the peace is lasting.

God's coming is announced before it happens. The voice does not describe the exiles' effort but calls for a way to be prepared for God, who is the one on the move. Every Gospel uses this verse to introduce the one who announced Jesus.

The passage sets the permanence of God's word against the transience of everything human, including the empires that seem permanent. It is the ground of the whole message: comfort can be spoken because the word that speaks it will not fail.

Knowing God's name means knowing him by what he does. The God who spoke beforehand (41:26) proves himself by acting, and his people learn his identity in the event of their rescue. In John's Gospel Jesus uses the same ‘I am he’ formula in ways that echo these chapters (John 8:24, 8:28, 13:19).

Jeremiah warns elsewhere against prophets who pass off their own dreams as God's word (23:25-32), yet here receives a message in sleep. The difference, in the book's own terms, is the source: the test of a prophecy is whether the LORD sent it, not the form in which it came.
God's word is the guarantee of his act. The nations will know the LORD not by argument but by seeing that what he said came to pass, the Bible's own test of true prophecy (Deuteronomy 18:22).

God's word creates what it commands. Preaching to the dead is not a futile act when God has promised to act through it. The chapter is the Old Testament's most vivid picture of the effective word, the same conviction as Isaiah 55:10-11.
Even a prophet needs the vision explained. Daniel's distress and his question show that revelation in Scripture engages the mind; it is not received by passive awe but by asking and being told.
